summary.text: A differential identity for the generating function yields a base three-term coefficient recurrence, which is iterated through transfer matrices; their composition and determinant identities produce the required recurrence with explicitly constructed auxiliary polynomials. Alternating signs at half-integers force all roots of these polynomials into the desired intervals, while reflection symmetry and affine rescaling give the symmetry of $P$, and evenness allows the second auxiliary polynomial to be written as $Q(x^2)$.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
p(t)=t^2-t+\frac15,
\qquad
c(t)=4(55t^4-34t^2+3).
\]
We shall construct the required polynomials from an auxiliary family of polynomials \(B_r\). The proof has four parts: a recurrence for the original sequence, construction and analysis of the \(B_r\), a transfer identity, and the final specialization.

Throughout, an empty product is understood to be \(1\).

## 1. A three-term recurrence for the original sequence

Put
\[
g(x)=\frac{1+x}{1-x}
\]
as a formal power series, and write
\[
e(n,j)=[x^j]g(x)^n.
\]
The sequence in the problem is
\[
a(n)=e(n,2n).
\]
This agrees with the usual binomial-sum description. Indeed,
\[
g(x)^n=(1+x)^n(1-x)^{-n},
\]
and, for \(n>0\),
\[
[x^r](1-x)^{-n}=\binom{n+r-1}{n-1}.
\]
Thus, after replacing the index \(i\) from the factor \((1+x)^n\) by \(k=n-i\),
\[
a(n)=\sum_{k=0}^n \binom nk\binom{2n+k-1}{n-1}.
\]
Also \(a(0)=1\).

We need two elementary coefficient identities. Since
\[
(1-x)g(x)=1+x,
\]
multiplication by \(g(x)^n\) and comparison of the coefficient of \(x^{j+1}\) gives
\[
e(n+1,j+1)-e(n+1,j)=e(n,j+1)+e(n,j). \tag{1}
\]
Next,
\[
(1-x^2)\frac{d}{dx}g(x)^{n}=2n g(x)^n.
\]
Comparing the coefficient of \(x^{j+1}\) gives, for every \(n,j\geq0\),
\[
(j+2)e(n,j+2)-j e(n,j)=2n e(n,j+1). \tag{2}
\]
(The case \(n=0\) is immediate, and the same displayed formula still holds.)

It is convenient to shift the sequence by defining
\[
s_0=-4,
\qquad
s_{k+1}=a(k)\quad(k\geq0).
\]
Then, for every integer \(N\geq0\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
&20\left(N+\frac12\right)(N+1)p(N)s_{N+2}\\
&\qquad-20\left(N-\frac12\right)(N-1)p(-N)s_N
=c(N)s_{N+1}. \tag{3}
\end{aligned}
\]
Here is a direct derivation. For \(N=0\), substitute \(s_0=-4\), \(s_1=a(0)=1\), \(s_2=a(1)=2\), and the identity follows. If \(N=k+1\), replace the three terms \(s_{N},s_{N+1},s_{N+2}\) by
\[
e(k,2k),\qquad e(k+1,2k+2),\qquad e(k+2,2k+4).
\]
Use (1) for \((n,j)=(k,2k),(k,2k+1),(k,2k+2),(k,2k+3)\) and for \((k+1,2k),\ldots,(k+1,2k+3)\), and use (2) for
\[
(k,2k),(k,2k+1),(k,2k+2),(k+1,2k),(k+2,2k).
\]
Successively eliminating the intermediate coefficients \(e(r,q)\) leaves
\[
20\left(k+\frac32\right)(k+2)p(k+1)e(k+2,2k+4)
-20\left(k+\frac12\right)k p(-k-1)e(k,2k)
=c(k+1)e(k+1,2k+2),
\]
which is (3). This elimination uses only addition and multiplication of the displayed relations (1) and (2), so it remains valid also at the small boundary values where some coefficients vanish.

We shall also repeatedly use
\[
p(-y)=p(y+1). \tag{4}
\]

## 2. The auxiliary polynomial family

The roots of \(p\) are
\[
\rho_1=\frac{5-\sqrt5}{10},
\qquad
\rho_2=\frac{5+\sqrt5}{10}.
\]
They are distinct and satisfy
\[
0<\rho_1<\rho_2<1. \tag{5}
\]
In particular, \(p(y)>0\) for \(y\leq0\) and for \(y\geq1\).

Define
\[
B_0(x)=0,
\qquad
B_1(x)=p(x+1),
\qquad
B_2(x)=c(x+1).
\]
For \(r\geq0\), the family is continued by the polynomial recurrence
\[
\begin{aligned}
&B_{r+2}(x)p(x+r+1)\\
&=c(x+r+1)B_{r+1}(x)
 +400\left(x+r+\frac12\right)^2(x+r)(x+r+1)
 p(-(x+r+1))B_r(x). \tag{6}
\end{aligned}
\]
We must justify that this really defines a polynomial \(B_{r+2}\), namely that the right side is divisible by \(p(x+r+1)\). It is useful to establish simultaneously the shifted companion identity
\[
\begin{aligned}
&B_{r+2}(y-1)p(y+1)\\
&=c(y)B_{r+1}(y)
 +400y\left(y+\frac12\right)^2(y+1)p(y)B_r(y+1). \tag{7}
\end{aligned}
\]

For \(r=0\), both (6) and (7) are immediate from \(B_0,B_1,B_2\). For \(r=1\), direct substitution shows that the proposed numerator for \(B_3\) vanishes at
\(ho_1-2\) and \(\rho_2-2\). Indeed, after using
\(\rho_i^2-\rho_i+1/5=0\), all remaining terms cancel. Since these are the two distinct roots of \(p(x+2)\), the numerator is divisible by \(p(x+2)\). This gives \(B_3\), (6) for \(r=1\), and then (7) for \(r=1\) by expansion and (4).

Now suppose (6) and (7) are known for \(r\) and \(r+1\). Define
\[
\begin{aligned}
F(y)&=c(y+r+2)B_{r+3}(y-1)\\
&\quad+400\left(y+r+\frac32\right)^2(y+r+1)(y+r+2)
 p(-(y+r+2))B_{r+2}(y-1),\\
G(y)&=c(y)B_{r+3}(y)
 +400y\left(y+\frac12\right)^2(y+1)p(y)B_{r+2}(y+1).
\end{aligned}
\]
Using the four induction hypotheses—(6) and (7) at the two consecutive indices—and collecting terms gives
\[
p(y+r+2)G(y)=p(y+1)F(y). \tag{8}
\]
Evaluate this at \(y=\rho_i-r-2\). The left side is zero. On the other hand,
\[
y+1=\rho_i-r-1\leq0,
\]
by (5), and hence \(p(y+1)>0\). Therefore \(F(y)=0\). Equivalently, the proposed numerator for \(B_{r+4}\) vanishes at both roots
\(ho_i-r-3\) of \(p(x+r+3)\). Thus it is divisible by that quadratic, proving that \(B_{r+4}\) is a polynomial and proving (6) at index \(r+2\). Equation (8), followed by cancellation of \(p(y+r+2)\), gives (7) at index \(r+2\).

There is no difficulty at the two zeros of the cancelled factor: both sides are polynomials, equality holds away from finitely many points, and therefore holds everywhere. This completes the simultaneous induction and establishes (6) and (7) for every \(r\geq0\).

### Symmetry of \(B_r\)

We claim
\[
B_r(-x-r)=B_r(x) \qquad(r\geq0). \tag{9}
\]
This is clear for \(r=0,1\). Assume it for \(r\) and \(r+1\). Apply (6) at \(-x-r-2\), and apply (7) at \(x+1\). Use the induction hypotheses to identify the occurrences of \(B_r\) and \(B_{r+1}\), and use (4). The resulting equations show
\[
p(x+2)B_{r+2}(-x-r-2)=p(x+2)B_{r+2}(x).
\]
Cancellation as a polynomial identity proves (9).

### Signs at half-integers

The crucial sign pattern is the following. For every \(r\geq1\) and every integer \(j\),
\[
\begin{cases}
B_r(-j/2)<0,&j\text{ odd and }0\leq j\leq2r,\\
B_r(-j/2)>0,&j\text{ even, or }j<0,\text{ or }j>2r.
\end{cases} \tag{10}
\]

For \(r=1\), this follows from \(B_1(-j/2)=p((2-j)/2)\): the only odd integer in \([0,2]\) is \(j=1\), where \(p(1/2)=-1/20\), while at every other relevant half-integer \(p\) is positive. For \(r=2\), use \(B_2(-j/2)=c((2-j)/2)\). One computes
\[
c(1/2)=c(-1/2)=-\frac{33}{4},
\]
and \(c(t/2)>0\) for every integer \(t\ne\pm1\). Hence (10) also holds for \(r=2\).

Suppose (10) holds for \(r\) and \(r+1\). To prove it for \(r+2\), write
\[
j=2r+2-t,
\]
where \(t\in\mathbb Z\), and apply (6) at \(x=-j/2\). If
\[
A_2=B_{r+2}(-j/2),\quad A_1=B_{r+1}(-j/2),\quad A_0=B_r(-j/2),
\]
then
\[
A_2p(t/2)=c(t/2)A_1+C(t)A_0, \tag{11}
\]
where
\[
C(t)=400\left(\frac{t-1}{2}\right)^2\left(\frac{t-2}{2}\right)
\left(\frac t2\right)p\left(\frac t2+1\right).
\]
For integer \(t\ne1\), \(p(t/2)>0\). Also \(c(t/2)>0\) except at \(t=\pm1\).

If \(t\geq3\), then \(C(t)>0\). When the desired conclusion is that \(A_2<0\), parity and the bounds translate through \(j=2r+2-t\) so that both \(A_1,A_0<0\) by the induction hypotheses; (11) then gives \(A_2<0\). In every remaining case in this range, both \(A_1,A_0>0\), and (11) gives \(A_2>0\).

If \(t\leq-3\), again \(C(t)>0\): the two linear factors \((t-2)/2\) and \(t/2\) are both negative, while \(p(t/2+1)>0\). Here the negative alternative in (10) is impossible, and the induction hypotheses give \(A_1,A_0>0\); thus \(A_2>0\).

It remains to check \(t=-2,-1,0,1,2\). Equation (11) becomes as follows.

* For \(t=-2\),
  \[
  \frac{11}{5}A_2=96A_1+360A_0,
  \]
  and both \(A_1,A_0\) are positive, so \(A_2>0\).
* For \(t=-1\),
  \[
  \frac{19}{20}A_2=-\frac{33}{4}A_1-15A_0.
  \]
  Both \(A_1,A_0\) are positive, so \(A_2<0\), exactly as required for the corresponding odd \(j\).
* For \(t=0\),
  \[
  \frac15A_2=12A_1,
  \]
  and \(A_1>0\), so \(A_2>0\).
* For \(t=1\),
  \[
  -\frac1{20}A_2=-\frac{33}{4}A_1.
  \]
  Here \(A_1<0\), so the right side is positive and \(A_2<0\).
* For \(t=2\),
  \[
  \frac15A_2=96A_1,
  \]
  and \(A_1>0\), so \(A_2>0\).

This proves (10) by induction.

### Degrees and zeros of \(B_r\)

From (6), \(\deg p=2\), \(\deg c=4\), and induction give
\[
\deg B_r\leq2r. \tag{12}
\]
Indeed, if the bounds for \(B_r,B_{r+1}\) are \(2r,2r+2\), then the numerator in (6) has degree at most \(2r+6\), and division by the monic quadratic \(p(x+r+1)\) leaves degree at most \(2r+4\).

Now consider the \(2r+1\) points
\[
-r,-r+\frac12,\ldots,-\frac12,0.
\]
By (10), the signs of \(B_r\) alternate at consecutive points. The intermediate value theorem therefore gives one zero in each of the \(2r\) intervening open intervals. These zeros are distinct and all lie in \((-r,0)\). Combined with (12), this proves that
\[
\deg B_r=2r \quad(r\geq1), \tag{13}
\]
and that all its complex zeros are real and belong to \((-r,0)\). To justify the last statement explicitly: a nonzero degree-\(2r\) polynomial has at most \(2r\) distinct zeros over \(\mathbb C\), while we have already found \(2r\) distinct real zeros.

For positive integers \(u,r\), define the affine transform
\[
G_{u,r}(X)=B_r(uX-u).
\]
It follows from (13) that \(G_{u,r}\) has degree \(2r\), and all its complex zeros are real and lie in
\[
1-\frac ru<X<1. \tag{14}
\]

## 3. Transfer matrices

Define
\[
D_r(x)=5^r\prod_{k=0}^{2r-1}(2x+1+k)\,p(x),
\]
\[
E_r(x)=(-5)^r\prod_{j=0}^{2r-1}(2x-2+j)\,p(x+r).
\]
They satisfy
\[
D_{r+1}(x)=D_r(x)\,5(2x+2r+1)(2x+2r+2), \tag{15}
\]
and
\[
E_{r+1}(x)p(x+r)=E_r(x)(-5)(2x+2r-2)(2x+2r-1)p(x+r+1). \tag{16}
\]
For nonnegative integers \(N\), \(D_r(N)>0\).

Introduce the matrix \(R_m(x)=(R_{ij}^{(m)}(x))\) by
\[
\begin{aligned}
R_{11}^{(m)}(x)&=B_{m+2}(x-1),\\
R_{12}^{(m)}(x)&=20(x-1)(x-\tfrac12)B_{m+1}(x),\\
R_{21}^{(m)}(x)&=20(x+m+\tfrac12)(x+m+1)B_{m+1}(x-1),\\
R_{22}^{(m)}(x)&=400(x-1)(x-\tfrac12)(x+m+\tfrac12)(x+m+1)B_m(x).
\end{aligned}
\]
Also put
\[
\widetilde M(y)=
\begin{pmatrix}
c(y)&20(y-1)(y-\tfrac12)p(y+1)\\
20(y+\tfrac12)(y+1)p(y)&0
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
For \(m=0\), the definitions of \(B_0,B_1,B_2\) give
\[
R_0(x)=\widetilde M(x). \tag{17}
\]
Equations (6) and (7), after multiplication by the displayed elementary factors, give the matrix relation
\[
p(x+m+1)R_{m+1}(x)=\widetilde M(x+m+1)R_m(x). \tag{18}
\]
Every one of the four entries in (18) is precisely (6) or (7), with a common elementary factor attached.

The base recurrence (3), together with (17), now yields the transfer formula
\[
D_{m+1}(N)
\binom{s_{N+m+2}}{s_{N+m+1}}
=R_m(N)\binom{s_{N+1}}{s_N} \tag{19}
\]
for all \(m,N\geq0\). Indeed, for \(m=0\), the first row is exactly (3), using (4), and the second row is an identity. If (19) holds for \(m\), multiply by \(\widetilde M(N+m+1)\), use (18), use (3) at \(N+m+1\), and then use (15). This gives (19) for \(m+1\).

We also need two structural consequences. Iterating (18), while accounting for the common factor at the joining point, gives
\[
p(x+m+1)R_{m+m'+1}(x)=R_{m'}(x+m+1)R_m(x) \tag{20}
\]
for all \(m,m'\geq0\). For \(m'=0\), this is (18). The induction step follows by applying (18) once more to the left factor; after multiplying by \(p(x+m+m'+2)\), the induction hypothesis gives the four matrix entries, and cancellation gives (20). Since all entries are polynomials, cancellation remains valid at the two roots of the factor.

Taking determinants in (18), using (15), (16), and the base case from (17), gives
\[
\det R_m(x)=D_{m+1}(x)E_{m+1}(x). \tag{21}
\]
More explicitly, the base case follows by direct evaluation of \(\det\widetilde M(x)\). In the induction step, the determinant of (18) multiplies \(\det R_m\) by the two off-diagonal factors of \(\widetilde M\); formulas (15) and (16) show that the resulting product is \(D_{m+2}E_{m+2}\). The two factors \(p(x+m+1)\) cancel as polynomial identities.

Combining the first two entry identities of (20) with \(m'=m\), and then using (21), gives the key identity
\[
\begin{aligned}
&B_{m+1}(x)B_{2m+3}(x-1)-B_{2m+2}(x)B_{m+2}(x-1)\\
&=-(-25)^{m+1}
 \prod_{k=0}^{2m+1}(2x+1+k)
 \prod_{j=0}^{2m+1}(2x+j)
 p(x)B_{m+1}(x+m+1). \tag{22}
\end{aligned}
\]
To see the elimination, multiply the first entry identity in (20) by
\(20(x-1)(x-\tfrac12)B_{m+1}(x)\), subtract the second entry identity multiplied by \(B_{m+2}(x-1)\), and replace the resulting \(2\times2\) minor by (21). Expanding
\[
E_{m+1}(x)=(-5)^{m+1}(2x-2)(2x-1)
\prod_{j=0}^{2m-1}(2x+j)p(x+m+1)
\]
and
\[
D_{m+1}(x)=5^{m+1}\prod_{k=0}^{2m+1}(2x+1+k)p(x)
\]
produces (22). Initially both sides have the common factor
\(20(x-1)(x-\tfrac12)p(x+m+1)\); cancellation away from its finitely many zeros, followed by polynomial continuity, proves (22) everywhere.

## 4. Construction of \(P,Q\), recurrence, and zeros

Fix the positive integer \(M\) from the statement. Define
\[
P_M(X)=5^M B_M(MX-M), \tag{23}
\]
and
\[
E_M(X)=B_{2M}(MX-M). \tag{24}
\]
By (9),
\[
P_M(1-X)=P_M(X), \tag{25}
\]
and
\[
E_M(-X)=E_M(X). \tag{26}
\]
Thus \(E_M\) is even, so there is a unique real polynomial \(Q_M\) such that
\[
Q_M(X^2)=E_M(X). \tag{27}
\]
Concretely, if \(E_M(X)=\sum d_jX^j\), all odd \(d_j\) vanish by (26), and
\(Q_M(T)=\sum d_{2j}T^j\).

By (13), \(P_M\) has degree \(2M\), while \(E_M\) has degree \(4M\). Therefore
\[
\deg P_M=\deg Q_M=2M. \tag{28}
\]

We now prove the recurrence. Let \(n\geq1\), write \(n=n'+1\), and set
\[
N_0=Mn'=M(n-1).
\]
Apply (19) first with \(m=M-1,N=N_0\), and then with \(m=2M-1,N=N_0\). Their first rows are
\[
D_M(N_0)s_{N_0+M+1}
=B_{M+1}(N_0-1)s_{N_0+1}
+20(N_0-1)(N_0-\tfrac12)B_M(N_0)s_{N_0}, \tag{29}
\]
and
\[
D_{2M}(N_0)s_{N_0+2M+1}
=B_{2M+1}(N_0-1)s_{N_0+1}
+20(N_0-1)(N_0-\tfrac12)B_{2M}(N_0)s_{N_0}. \tag{30}
\]
In the indexing used by \(s_{r+1}=a(r)\), these three significant values are
\[
s_{N_0+2M+1}=a(M(n+1)),\quad
s_{N_0+M+1}=a(Mn),\quad
s_{N_0+1}=a(M(n-1)).
\]
Equivalently, if \(b(n)=a(Mn)\), they are \(b(n+1),b(n),b(n-1)\).

Multiply (30) by \(B_M(N_0)\), multiply (29) by \(B_{2M}(N_0)\), and subtract. The terms involving \(s_{N_0+1}\) are simplified by (22), with \(m=M-1\) and \(x=N_0\). Also split
\[
D_{2M}(N_0)=D_M(N_0)\left(5^M\prod_{k=0}^{2M-1}(2N_0+2M+1+k)\right). \tag{31}
\]
Since \(D_M(N_0)>0\), it can be cancelled. Using
\[
P_M(n)=5^M B_M(N_0), \tag{32}
\]
which follows from \(Mn-M=N_0\), symmetry (9) gives
\[
P_M(-n)=5^M B_M(N_0+M). \tag{33}
\]
Furthermore, (27) gives
\[
Q_M(n^2)=E_M(n)=B_{2M}(N_0). \tag{34}
\]
Finally, simple reindexing of the products gives
\[
\prod_{k=1}^{2M}(2Mn+k)
=\prod_{k=0}^{2M-1}(2N_0+2M+1+k), \tag{35}
\]
and
\[
\prod_{k=1}^{2M}(2Mn-k)
=\prod_{j=0}^{2M-1}(2N_0+j). \tag{36}
\]
Substitution of (31)–(36) into the subtraction of (29) from (30), together with
\[
(-1)^M5^M=(-5)^M,
\qquad
5^M(-5)^M=(-25)^M,
\]
yields exactly
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\left(\prod_{k=1}^{2M}(2Mn+k)\right)P_M(n)b(n+1)\\
&\quad+(-1)^M\left(\prod_{k=1}^{2M}(2Mn-k)\right)P_M(-n)b(n-1)
=Q_M(n^2)b(n). \tag{37}
\end{aligned}
\]
This holds for every \(n\geq1\).

It remains only to verify the asserted locations of the zeros. By (14), with \(u=r=M\), every complex zero of \(B_M(MX-M)\), and hence of \(P_M\), is real and lies strictly between \(0\) and \(1\). In particular all zeros of \(P_M\) lie in the closed interval \([0,1]\).

Similarly, apply (14) with \(u=M,r=2M\). Every complex zero of
\[
E_M(X)=B_{2M}(MX-M)
\]
is real and lies strictly between \(-1\) and \(1\). If a complex number \(z\) is a zero of \(Q_M(z^2)\), then by (27) it is a zero of \(E_M(z)\); hence \(z\) is real and \(-1<z<1\). Thus all zeros of \(Q_M(X^2)\) are real and lie in \([-1,1]\).

Taking \(P=P_M\) and \(Q=Q_M\), equations (25), (28), and (37), together with the two root-location conclusions, prove every assertion of the conjecture.
